messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Short answer**

If you’re only interested in how far the car moves *horizontally* during a given time \(t\), the distance is simply

\[
x(t)=v\,\cos\theta \; t .
\]

If you want the full two‑dimensional displacement (the “arc” the car traces in that time), you need both components:

\[
\begin{aligned}
x(t)&=v\,\cos\theta \; t,\\[4pt]
y(t)&=v\,\sin\theta \; t-\tfrac12 g\,t^{2},
\end{aligned}
\]

so the magnitude of the displacement vector is

\[
d(t)=\sqrt{\bigl(v\,\cos\theta \; t\bigr)^{2}+\bigl(v\,\sin\theta \; t-\tfrac12 g\,t^{2}\bigr)^{2}} .
\]

---

### Why the horizontal component is \(v\cos\theta\,t\)

In projectile motion the horizontal velocity component is constant (ignoring air resistance).  
If the car is launched with speed \(v\) at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, the horizontal component of its velocity is

\[
v_x = v\cos\theta .
\]

Because this component doesn’t change, the horizontal distance covered in a time interval \(t\) is just

\[
x = v_x\,t = v\cos\theta\,t .
\]

---

### When you want the *range* (distance until the car lands)

If you’re actually looking for the total horizontal distance the car travels from launch until it returns to the same vertical level (i.e., the “range”), you first need the time of flight:

\[
t_{\text{flight}} = \frac{2\,v\sin\theta}{g},
\]

where \(g\approx9.81\;\text{m/s}^2\) is the acceleration due to gravity.  
Plugging that into the horizontal distance formula gives the classic result

\[
\boxed{R = \frac{v^{2}\sin(2\theta)}{g}} .
\]

---

### Quick reference table

| Quantity | Formula | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| Horizontal distance in time \(t\) | \(x(t)=v\cos\theta\,t\) | Constant horizontal speed |
| Vertical position in time \(t\) | \(y(t)=v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12 g t^{2}\) | Gravity pulls down |
| Total displacement magnitude in time \(t\) | \(d(t)=\sqrt{[v\cos\theta\,t]^{2}+[v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12 g t^{2}]^{2}}\) | Arc length of the trajectory |
| Range (until landing) | \(R=\dfrac{v^{2}\sin(2\theta)}{g}\) | Time of flight \(t_{\text{flight}}=2v\sin\theta/g\) |

Feel free to plug in your numbers for \(v\), \(\theta\), and \(t\) to get the exact distance!
